source.title: Consensus Control for Decentralized Deep Learning
source.authors: Lingjing Kong; Tao Lin; Anastasia Koloskova; Martin Jaggi; Sebastian U. Stich

record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally tests how decentralized training and consensus distance affect training and test performance, using methods different from the listed versions. Its results do not test any of V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The study varies consensus distance and training phase and reports test accuracy, but does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, CNN versus fully connected architectures, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. Its discussion of prior work is not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study tests consensus distance and communication timing, which are outside V1–V8. It uses learning-rate scaling and warmup from the V5 literature as training tools. Appendix D explicitly sets extreme large-batch difficulties outside its scope. Its Adam experiments compare communication schemes, not Adam against SGD; its smoothness measurements do not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or rank generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors identify consensus distance as central to decentralized training, show theoretically that sufficiently small consensus distance preserves centralized optimization rates, and empirically find that early consensus control can recover centralized test performance while some middle-phase disagreement improves it. The generalization conclusions are empirical, primarily for data-center training with i.i.d. data; middle-phase improvements are setting dependent.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies decentralized gossip averaging and phase-specific consensus distance, rather than testing the listed memorization, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, sharpness, or memorized-example interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Consensus distance and the training phase in which decentralization is applied change test performance; dataset and worker count also distinguish reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Early consensus control improves decentralized training performance. For CIFAR-10 with 32 workers, reducing the phase-1 target from Ξmax to one quarter raises test accuracy from 91.78% to 92.74%, against 92.82% centrally. Phase-2 decentralization reaches 93.04%. ImageNet-32 shows early-phase recovery, but middle-phase improvement over its centralized baseline is not consistent across worker counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consensus distance affects decentralized neural-network generalization differently across training phases: sufficiently tight early consensus can recover centralized performance, while some middle-phase disagreement can improve it.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 139, 2021
record.problems: The study reports three seeds for most CIFAR-10 results and two seeds for ImageNet-32 results; ImageNet-32 experiments are constrained by compute budget. The Transformer study is described as preliminary. No random-label or arbitrary-label capability check is conducted.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported outcomes are omitted to keep extraction focused: Table 1's uncontrolled topology comparison; Table 5–19 results on phase combinations, training duration, topology, local-estimate consensus control and optimizer additions; figure-only learning curves and consensus measurements; and the Transformer validation-loss curves. These are in the cited tables/figures in Sections 4–5 and Appendices A and E.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance performance on held-out random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning, including remedies for any performance difference.
A large-batch penalty under fixed epoch budgets and its removal by recipe adaptations; scaling and warmup are used without testing these propositions.
Effects of adding or removing dropout, including training-set size, underfitting and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps and its ranking against other measures.
Accuracy after removing examples selected by label memorization versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted table values and baselines match the supplied text. States are changed to cannot_determine because no row measures a listed version, rather than because the accuracies are unreadable. Worker-count comparisons also change global batch size, but the study does not isolate an extreme-batch penalty or evaluate a remedy against an unadapted batch-size control. The local smoothness curves concern optimization dynamics, not V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure. Other consensus-control results and Transformer curves are already declared in rows_left_out and do not require missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning and weight-decay choices.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
Removing examples selected for memorization and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
